Kaṭha Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The Kaṭha Upaniṣad belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Since it is included in the Kāṭhaka recension of that Veda, it is also called Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad.
The story of नचिकेतस् and यम (the god of death) is very ancient and finds a mention even in the Ṛgveda (10.135). The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (

) gives an outline of the same story. In this Upaniṣad, the story gets a fuller treatment. Actually the whole work is in the form of a dialogue between नचिकेतस् and यम. It is spread over six vallīs or sections and the total number of verses is 119.
First vallī (29 verses)
Vājaśravasa, also known as Auddālaki आरुणि, was performing the विश्वजित् sacrifice. He was, as per the rules of the sacrifice, to give away all his wealth. However, he had arranged to donate decrepit, useless cows as sacrificial gifts. This was observed by नचिकेतस्, his young son in early boyhood. A precocious boy that he was, he sensed his ड़थेर्’s motive in doing so. Wishing to draw his attention, to this lacuna, नचिकेतस् asked his ड़थेर् as to whom he was being gifted away. Incensed by the repeated questioning, the ड़थेर् shot back saying that he would be given to मृत्यु (Yama, the god of death). Though he repented for his intemperate reaction, he allowed नचिकेतस् to go to the यमलोक, the abode of यम. When the boy reached there यम was not in his होउसे. So he patiently awaited the god’s return, spending three days and three nights without accepting any होस्पितलित्य्. When यम returned and learnt about the young guest, he regretted the inconvenience caused to him and offered him three boons to compensate for the same.
Naciketas asked, as the first boon, that his ड़थेर् regain his mental peace and balance and also recognize him (Naciketas) after returning from the abode of death.
As the second, he requested यम to teach him the sacrifice by which one could go to svargaloka (heaven). यम obliged and taught the process in detail. He even tested नचिकेतस् at the end to know whether he had grasped all the intricacies of the ritual. नचिकेतस्’ reply so pleased him that he granted him (Naciketas) an additional boon in the form of a beautiful necklace. He also christened the fire-ritual as ‘Nāciketāgni’.
As the last of the boons, नचिकेतस् asked यम whether a human being continued in existence even after the death of the physical body, or not. Since this question related to आत्मज्ञान or a know-ledge of the divine Self which was extremely subtle and difficult to comprehend, यम wanted to test the boy thoroughly before imparting the same. Acquisition of आत्मज्ञान has to be preceded by an intense spirit of renunciation and total dedication to its pursuit. Hence यम tried to dissuade him by describing it as extremely difficult to comprehend and offered exceedingly attractive alternatives like immense wealth, intense pleasures and unimaginably long life. However, नचिकेतस् being made of sterner stuff, rejected them all with disdain and insisted upon his original boon.
Second Vallī (25 verses)
Yama does not directly answer the question of नचिकेतस् but begins his long discourse by introducing some basic concepts as a background.
Human beings generally have two alternatives in life: the श्रेयस् (what is really good in the ultimate analysis) and the प्रेयस् (what is momentarily attractive and pleasant, but ultimately disastrous). The wise ones with an intuitive insight choose the former whereas the dull-witted persons who lack even elementary sense of discrimination, fall for the latter. Having done so, these latter ones consider themselves as very intelligent and clever. Not only that, they even mislead the innocent persons. It is like the blind leading the other blind ones! Thus they get into the grip of the lord of death through repeated transmigrations.
Those who choose the path of श्रेयस् will realize the आत्मन्, the true self of all.
This आत्मन् is beyond लोगिच् and reasoning and is difficult to comprehend by the ordinary run of mankind. But it can be understood if taught by a person who has realised his identity with it. It is hidden deep within oneself and can be attained by adhyātmayoga, योग of inner contemplation.
Yama then expounds the art of meditation on the आत्मन्/Brahman with the help of प्रणव or Om. Om is the best symbol for ब्रह्मन् and also the best means for attaining that ब्रह्मन्.
Ātman/Brahman is smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest. It is also established in the hearts of all. It can be realised by the pure, calm and controlled मिन्द्. One who realises it goes beyond death and rebirth.
Neither the study of the scriptures and encyclopaedic knowledge nor the retentive power of memory can help in attaining the आत्मन्. Only an intense desire to know it, can make the seeker succeed in his efforts.
Yama also stresses the importance of a clean moral life and of self-control in this endeavour.
Third Vallī (17 verses)
The most important teaching of this section is the allegory of the chariot to describe the jīvātman, the individual सोउल् enmeshed in the body-मिन्द् complex. The body is the chariot. The senses are the horses. The मिन्द् is the reins. The intellect is the charioteer. The Self is the master of the chariot. The objects of the senses are the road by which the chariot moves.
If the horses are controlled by an expert charioteer, he can take the chariot to the right destination. An inefficient charioteer and restive horses will lead the chariot astray into a ditch and endanger the life of its owner.
Similarly one who can control his senses through a disciplined मिन्द् will reach the final goal of his life, viz., the abode of विष्णु (i.e., लिबेरतिओन्). On the other hand, a person of impure मिन्द् and uncontrolled senses will end up in सṁसार or transmigration.
The आत्मन् or the Self, also called ‘puruṣa’ (divine being), who is deeply hidden in one’s heart can be seen or realised by a person of refined and subtle मिन्द् through concentration. For this, one has to awaken to this reality and approach the great spiritual teachers, to learn from them, because, the path that leads to this आत्मन् is extremely difficult to tread.
Fourth Vallī (15 Verses)
This vallī starts with a statement of fact that our senses always tend to go outwards and consequently we are inte-rested in the outside world. However, once in a while, some wise person discovers that what is really worth knowing in life is the प्रत्यगात्मन्, the Self within. Hence he turns the gaze of the senses and the मिन्द् inwards and realises him there. But the ignorant, childish persons continue to revel in the outside world of sense-objects and get into the bondage of transmigration.
Yama then declares that it is possible to realise the आत्मन् through the pure and refined मिन्द्.
Yama describes the आत्मन् residing in the hearts of all, as of the size of the thumb, since the heart is of that size. Even so, he is the lord of the past, present and future (because, in the ultimate analysis he is ब्रह्मन्).
Once a person realises this आत्मन्, he becomes united with him even as one pure water mixed with another pure water becomes identical with it.
Fifth Vallī (15 verses)
This short section begins by describing the human body as a pura or city in which the आत्मन्, its lord lives. meditation on him delivers one from the bondage of transmigration.
Then comes an interesting, even poetical, account of that आत्मन्: He moves every where. He is the sun and the मोओन्. He exists in every object of the universe. He manages the biological functions of the body from inside. In fact, it is his residence in the body that makes it full of life and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
Then there is a description of the transmigration of the unredeemed souls. Their next lives are determined by their कर्म, good or bad. If some are reborn as living beings of the higher or the lower type, others may even enter inert objects!
Quoting the examples of fire, air and the sun, the Upaniṣad goes on to describe that ब्रह्मन् as the inner Self (anta-rātman) of all beings, seems to appear in different forms, identifies with those forms, and also simultaneously exists in his own, outside them. Even as the sun, while shining on all objects—pure and impure—himself remains untainted, ब्रह्मन् too remains untainted for ever.
Only those who realise this आत्मन्/ ब्रह्मन्, succeed in attaining everlasting peace and not the others.
Sixth Vallī (18 verses)
This last vallī sets out with the description of the सṁसार vṛkṣa, the tree of the world, in a poetical language. It is an inverted tree, with the root above and the branches below. This root is ब्रह्मन्.
This ब्रह्मन्, (also called प्राण here) the origin and power of sustenance of the whole च्रेअतिओन्, is so terrific that it strikes fear in the hearts of all, functioning as a part of this universe. The sun shines, the fire burns and the wind blows out of his fear. While इन्द्र discharges his duties, मृत्यु or the god of death just runs away!
The Upaniṣad then urges all human beings to realise this आत्मन्/Brahman before the fall of the body. It also declares the superiority of the आत्मन् over all other aspects of the body and the मिन्द्. It gives a brief account of योग as self-control and concentration by which the आत्मन् is realised. For this, it is necessary to conquer and destroy all the desires in the मिन्द्. Once this is done, man becomes immortal.
Here, the text brings in the idea well-known in the other उपनिषद्स् also, that the realised सोउल् leaves by the nāḍī (subtle tubular structure) in the crown of the head, which is connected with the arcirādimārga (or the bright path, the path of light) and goes to ब्रह्मलोक, the Abode of ब्रह्मन्, never to return again to the mundane existence.
For this realisation, one must know the art of separating the Self from the body even as the stalk of the muñja grass is drawn out of its sheath. This can be done by a direct experience of the inner Self, the आत्मन्, through the knowledge that he is pure and deathless, immortal.
The last verse of the Upaniṣad gives us encouragement and hope, and also instils confidence in us. ब्रह्मविद्या and मोक्ष or amṛtattva (liberation and इम्मोर्तलित्य्) were not the special prerogative of नचिकेतस् or persons like him (who had the courage and conviction to go to the world of यम and return alive) but of all of us, provided we too know the path from competent persons and practise adhyātmayoga properly.
From all standpoints this Upaniṣad has been quite popular. The philosophical concepts and the practical modes of sādhanā described here are reminiscent of the popular Hindu scripture, the Bhagavadgītā.

Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtras
------------------------------------------
The गृह्यसूत्रस् are a part of the कल्प or Kalpasūtra literature, which itself is one of the six वेदाङ्गस् (subsidiary literature that aids the study of the वेदस्). The Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtras is one of the four गृह्यसूत्रस् belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It is also known by other names such as Carakagṛhya, Cārāyaṇīyagṛhya and Laugākṣigṛhya.
This work has been quoted by others, like हेमाद्रि (13th century A. D.). Since it has five khaṇḍas or chapters, it is also called Gṛhyapañcikā. Three commentaries have been discovered so far. They are: Vivaraṇa of Ādityadarśana, Paddhati of Brāhmaṇabala and Bhāṣya of Devapāla.
The contents are very similar to those of the other गृह्यसूत्रस् like those of आपस्तम्ब or बौधायन.

Kāṭhaka Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
The Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda has four शाखास् or recensions. The Kāṭhaka Saṁhitā (or Kaṭha Saṁhitā) is the third in that series.
Not many followers of this Saṁhitā are found now, even in South India which is the home of Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
This work has five kāṇḍas or sections. These kāṇḍas are, again, divided into subsections known as ‘sthānakas’.
A brief description of the same may now be given:
Kāṇḍa Sthānakas Contents
1. Iṭhimikākāṇḍa 18 puroḍāśa (rice-cake), अध्वर, some yāgas like वाजपेय and राजसूय.
2. Madhyamikā-kāṇḍa 12 Sāvitrī, स्वर्ग (heaven), dīkṣita (consecrated sacri-ficer), āyuṣyahoma and so on.
3, 4 and 5. Oramikākāṇḍa 10 Sattra, चातुर्मास्य, sava, Sautrāyaṇī etc.

The five kāṇḍas with forty sthānakas contain in all, 3091 mantras.
(Note: Details of the technical terms used here may be found under the particular headings.)

Kaṭharudropaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The Kaṭharudropaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad classed among those belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It has 47 mantras, both in prose and in ślokas. It is mainly devoted to सṁन्यास or monastic life and its fruit, viz., the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्.
It is in the form of a dialogue between the gods and प्रजापति. In reply to the request of the gods to teach about brahma-विद्या, प्रजापति expatiates on सṁन्यास and its result.
A householder who desired to take to the life of a saṁnyāsin (monk) should ceremonially give up all the insignias of a ब्राह्मण like the śikhā (tuft of hair), यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) and the Vedic fires.
He should hand over the responsibilities of the family to the eldest son.
While taking leave of the family members, he should not shed tears! (Nor should they!)
Then, the Upaniṣad describes briefly how a person should pass through the first two stages of life—brahmacarya and gārhasthya—and then renounce all things connected with them.
A saṁnyāsin should not kindle the Vedic fires again. He should desire the well-being of all persons. He should move about without any fixed place for dwelling, living on alms only. He must also renounce all possessions which are normally allowed for the lower type of saṁnyāsins, like the कमण्डलु (water bowl), pādukās (footwear), kanthā (covering cloth) and so on.
He is also expected to observe ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy) very strictly.
The Upaniṣad ends with a long description of the fruit of ब्रह्मज्ञान or knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, which is the same as is normally found in other उपनिषद्स्.
